notes: Analog of the real campaign's first RCE commands (Day 1, 04:01 UTC: `id`, `env`). Alone, indistinguishable from any of thousands of routine honeypot recon attempts -- matches #154's own framing that isolated low-signal events are the point.

Same session as corpus-001 (shared session ID is the correlation signal phase 2/3 should pick up on) -- config-file/hostname discovery, the recon step immediately preceding secret discovery in the real campaign's own sequence.

Benign near-neighbor: the single most common opportunistic-scanner command sequence this honeypot sees, from an unrelated session/source. Surface-identical shape to corpus-001 (recon commands over cowrie) but no follow-through -- exists to measure false positives on 'looks like recon' alone.

Benign near-neighbor for the source_control_ci_probe phase below (corpus-026): an actual real-shaped Dependabot PR (actor dependabot[bot], branch prefix dependabot/, standard bump title). Exactly the case dependabot-auto-merge.yml's own `github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]' && pull_request.user.login == 'dependabot[bot]'` guard is designed to allow.

Benign near-neighbor for the cloud_k8s_identity_probe phase below: a real operator (named actor, not 'unknown') requesting a narrow, short-lived introspection token through the dashboard's own settings UI -- narrow scope and short TTL are the discriminators against a broad/long-lived pattern.

Benign near-neighbor for the encoded_dropper_c2 phase below: an entirely ordinary, legitimate CI artifact upload that also happens to be gzip+base64 encoded (a completely standard compression choice) -- exists because 'the payload is encoded' alone is a weak signal; encoding plus destination plus actor is what should matter.

Benign near-neighbor for the internal_network_pivot phase below: APIARY's own real, expected WireGuard handshake between the VPS and homeserver (the actual production tunnel this stack relies on, per docs/honeypot-network-isolation.md) -- known peer identity and known tunnel IP range (10.8.0.0/24) are the discriminators against an unexpected mesh client.

notes: Benign near-neighbor for the exfiltration phase below: legitimate internal metrics telemetry, also base64-encoded POST, but both endpoints are internal (192.0.2.0/24 to 192.0.2.0/24, not crossing out to an external dead-drop) -- the destination boundary is the discriminator, not the encoding.

Benign near-neighbor for the persistence_self_migration phase below: APIARY's own real autoheal service restarting an unhealthy container -- same 'container lifecycle event acting across the fleet' shape, but through the narrow, allowlisted docker-socket-proxy path (see #592/docs/agent-intrusion-threat-model.md item 5), a named, expected actor, and no privilege escalation.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: environment variables dumped to stdout, including any secret-shaped ones

notes: Direct analog of the real campaign's HDF5 Vector 1 finding (/proc/self/environ read leaking pod secrets/tokens) and the threat model's own item 3 finding (plain-env secrets readable this way). Same session as corpus-001/002 -- this is where a real correlation engine should start raising severity, since it's the third event from the same actor within minutes, now touching a genuine secret-exposure boundary.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: attempted read of a projected service-account-identity token path

notes: Synthetic analog of the real campaign's Day 3 10:10 Kubernetes service-account token read. docs/agent-intrusion-threat-model.md item 4 found APIARY has no real Kubernetes -- this event is included anyway because the corpus's job is testing whether the pipeline recognizes the *signature* of this technique class (a workload-identity-token read attempt) regardless of whether it would succeed here; a honeypot session attempting it is real signal about the attacker's own toolkit even when the path predictably returns nothing.

Benign near-neighbor: a routine, legitimate scheduled job reading a sensitive-looking path (/etc/passwd) as part of an ordinary backup -- same 'sensitive file read' shape as corpus-010/011 above, actor is 'system' not an interactive session, no honeypot involvement at all.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: decompresses to a single inert marker command: echo corpus-marker-1

notes: Direct analog of the real campaign's own documented payload-packing convention, quoted verbatim in its technical writeup: `gzip.decompress(base64.b64decode("<blob>"))`, standardized at Day 1 19:32 UTC. The base64 blob here is a synthetic placeholder -- never a functional payload.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: would evaluate a Jinja2 SSTI payload if fed to a vulnerable template renderer

notes: Analog of the real campaign's Vector 2 (Jinja2 template injection into fsspec reference:// offset fields, achieving RCE via cycler.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.exec). docs/agent-intrusion-threat-model.md item 2 found *no* server-side template engine in this tree ever renders attacker-controlled strings -- should_escalate is false here specifically to encode that finding: this technique class has nowhere to land in APIARY today, so a correlation engine correctly treating it as inert (not zero-signal, since it's still an attempted RCE probe caught by the honeypot -- but not a crossed trust boundary) is the *correct* behavior to test for, not a gap.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: part 1 of a 3-part staged payload, reassembles to an inert marker script once all sequence numbers are collected

notes: Analog of the real campaign's own improvised message protocol (its writeup's exact words: type/channel/sequence-number/checksum fields, chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key, POSTed to a dumb public capture service). New source IP/session from corpus-001-014's actor -- self-migration/fresh-identity behavior, matching the campaign's own 'ephemeral by design' finding.

notes: Second chunk of the same multi-part message as corpus-015 -- same channel ID (c9f2), sequence incremented. Tests whether phase 2's decoder correctly reassembles by (channel, sequence) rather than treating each chunk as an independent event.

notes: DNS-based exfiltration alternate channel -- represents the real campaign's own 'multiple egress paths (interchangeable transports)' finding: the same data exfiltrated over HTTP POST (corpus-017) also shows up encoded into DNS query labels moments later, testing whether correlation groups these as the *same* exfil event via shared decoded content rather than as two unrelated alerts on two different sensors.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: a privileged container with the full host filesystem bind-mounted

notes: Analog of the real campaign's Day 3 19:53 UTC 'bare privileged pod with host filesystem mounted, achieving root on node' step, expressed in this stack's own Docker-Compose terms rather than a Kubernetes pod spec -- APIARY's real equivalent trust boundary is exactly this shape (see docs/agent-intrusion-threat-model.md item 5's own finding on raw docker.sock access being root-equivalent).

expected_findings.decoded_summary: second node in the same fleet-creation pattern as corpus-019

notes: Second host (192.0.2.51, vs corpus-019's 192.0.2.50) receiving the identical privileged-container pattern within two minutes -- the 'fleet across multiple nodes' shape from the real campaign's own Day 3 finding, testing whether correlation groups by *pattern* across hosts, not just by single-host repetition.

alert.signature: LOCAL Link-Local Metadata Service Access Attempt

expected_findings.decoded_summary: attempted GET to the link-local cloud metadata address from a non-cloud host

notes: Analog of the real campaign's Day 3 cloud-metadata credential harvesting (169.254.169.254 replay). docs/agent-intrusion-threat-model.md item 4 confirms APIARY's homeserver is bare-metal, not cloud VM-backed -- this request would simply time out/refuse here, but the *attempt* from an internal workload is itself strong signal (nothing legitimate on this stack ever has reason to address 169.254.169.254), which is exactly why should_escalate is true even though the technique cannot succeed on this infrastructure.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: a request to mint a broadly-scoped, 24-hour identity token

notes: Analog of the real campaign's forged 24-hour service-account tokens (minted using a harvested signing key). No real workload-identity-token minting endpoint exists in APIARY today -- included as a forward-looking corpus entry: if this stack ever grows one (a phase 4 candidate control point), this is the shape a criticality rule should catch on sight, broad scope + long TTL from an unexpected actor -- contrast with corpus-005's narrow-scope, short-TTL, named-operator baseline.

expected_findings.decoded_summary: a mesh-VPN client enrolling in memory-only mode with logging disabled and a local SOCKS5 proxy

notes: Direct analog of the real campaign's Day 4 mesh-VPN enrollment from the compromised sandbox, using the exact flag shapes its own writeup quotes (--state=mem:, --no-logs-no-support) to run a client in userspace with a SOCKS5 proxy. APIARY's own real infrastructure uses WireGuard for its VPS<->homeserver tunnel (docs/honeypot-network-isolation.md) -- this event tests whether an *unexpected* additional mesh client enrolling from a workload that has no legitimate reason to (192.0.2.50, not the known VPS/homeserver tunnel endpoints in corpus-007's own baseline) gets caught, which is the actual control APIARY needs regardless of which VPN technology a real attacker used.
